cards.title: Treat AEO as an SEO extension, not a new channel
cards.summary: LLM answer optimization overlaps heavily with SEO; the difference is mostly citation optimization, with different head and tail dynamics.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate content, technical SEO and optimization budget across classic search vs. ChatGPT/LLM answers for your product catalog or content.
steps: Recognize that the source argues SEO and AEO are not fundamentally different channels; the core technology is similar, so existing SEO infrastructure, crawlability and content quality work still apply.
Focus the incremental AEO effort on citation optimization: getting your pages selected as the source an LLM cites, rather than on a separate stack of tactics.
Account for the structural difference the source names: the head (broad, high-volume terms) and the tail (long, obscure queries) behave differently in LLM answers than in classic search rankings.
Be skeptical of vendors selling AEO as a wholly new channel with proprietary tools; the source attributes much of that framing to commercial incentive rather than technical difference.
Keep your classic SEO fundamentals running while adding citation-focused work, rather than replacing one with the other.
caveats: This is the presenter's assessment of overlap, not a measured equivalence; the head/tail divergence is described qualitatively.
AEO tooling and LLM interfaces change frequently — verify current behavior before committing budget.

cards.title: Track the AEO growth curve shape, not just its size
cards.summary: The AEO channel's adoption curve had an unusual dead period followed by a very steep January inflection, driven by LLM adoption and clickable rich modules.
cards.use_when: Timing when to invest in LLM-answer optimization for your store versus waiting for the channel to mature.
steps: Note the source's observation that the channel's interest curve was atypical: an initial webinar spike, then a flat period from roughly July to January where growth people saw little impact, then a sharp jump in January.
Attribute the inflection to two factors: increased everyday LLM adoption and increased clickability of answers, especially for commerce, local and hotels where rich modules let users click through.
For ecommerce specifically, the source says commerce answers gained clickable rich modules, meaning a citation can now produce traffic rather than just visibility.
Use the steepness of the curve as a signal that the channel moved faster than a typical new channel, so earlier experimentation carries less risk of wasted effort than the flat period suggested.
Re-check current clickability for your category (product, local, travel) before assuming the same click-through behavior applies.
caveats: The timeline and attribution are the presenter's field observations, not a controlled measurement.
Clickability varies by query type and engine; do not assume commerce answers always render clickable modules.

cards.title: Skip fully automated AI content; use AI-assisted, human-edited content
cards.summary: A large study found only ~10–12% of cited content in Google and ChatGPT is AI-generated while ~90% is not, indicating unassisted AI content does not win citations.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to mass-generate product descriptions, buying guides or category copy with AI for your store.
steps: Interpret 'AI-generated content' as automated content with no human in the loop; that is the specific thing the study tested and found ineffective.
The source's study pulled thousands of searches and questions, collected the Google results and ChatGPT citations, and ran an AI detector (Surfer SEO's) across them.

They validated the detector by generating thousands of AI articles and sampling 100,000 Common Crawl URLs from before ChatGPT launched, finding roughly an 8% false positive rate — supporting detector accuracy.
Result: about 10–12% of content ranking or cited was AI-generated, roughly 90% was not, and a correlation analysis showed the same pattern.

Apply this by treating AI as a drafting and editing aid: use it to accelerate research, outlines and first drafts, then have a human edit for accuracy, specificity and usefulness before publishing product or guide content.
Do not publish bulk unedited AI product copy or landing pages expecting it to rank or get cited.
caveats: The study measured correlation between AI-detected content and ranking/citation, not causation.
AI detectors are imperfect; the source reports an ~8% false positive rate, so some flagged content may be human-written.
This is one firm's study; results may shift as engines and detectors change — re-verify before basing a full content strategy on it.

cards.title: Expect AI-generated content to collapse citation diversity (model collapse risk)
cards.summary: If purely AI-generated content dominated, the source argues it would degrade into a self-summarizing loop and converge answers to a single opinion, like 'vanilla is the only flavor'.
cards.use_when: Evaluating the long-term risk of an AI-content-heavy content strategy for your store's category pages and buying guides.
steps: Understand the two places derivatives enter a system: the core model training and the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) layer that supplies citations.
A published paper on 'model collapse' showed that training a core model on its own derivatives quickly breaks it — producing hallucinations and failures.
The source ran a RAG-side study: generate 10 derivative articles, put them into rankings, summarize, then generate 10 more and summarize the summaries in an infinite loop.
The result: answers converge on a single opinion. The wisdom-of-the-crowd effect (averaging many diverse opinions beats the best single individual) shrinks to one answer.

The analogous incentive argument: if scraped or generated content worked, everyone would do it, and engines would eventually have to suppress derivatives — as Google did to shopping comparison sites in 2007.

For an ecommerce operator, the practical takeaway is to keep original, first-hand content (real product testing, real customer questions, real usage photos/data) that cannot be produced by re-summarizing others.
caveats: This is a reasoned scenario the source describes, supported by a model-collapse paper and an internal RAG study, not a prediction with a date.
The 'vanilla' ice cream example is an illustration, not a measured outcome.

cards.title: Optimize the help center as an AEO asset
cards.summary: Help center content frequently answers the 'can you do X / do you support Y' follow-up questions people ask LLMs, making it an underused AEO surface.
cards.use_when: Auditing your store's support and FAQ content to capture LLM-answer citations for feature, integration and use-case questions.
steps: Recognize that in chat, users ask follow-up questions about tools, features, use cases and integrations — questions typically answered in a help center, not a marketing page.
Move the help center from a subdomain to a subdirectory; the source says subdomains do not work well for this and subdirectories perform better.
Fix internal linking: help center pages are usually poorly internally linked. Add cross-links between related help center pages so the cluster is crawlable and connected.
Fill in the tail: you likely have help center articles for head terms but none for narrow, obscure use cases. Use sales call questions and customer support tickets to find those tails.

Example the source gives: no meeting-transcription tool integrates directly with Looker, but a workaround via Otter's Zapier integration into BigQuery could be documented — a non-zero-demand question with no existing article.
Open a community Q&A so users can surface tail questions you would never have anticipated, and answer them on your own site.
Note that common helpdesk tools (Zendesk, Intercom, etc.) should support these two changes; verify current subdirectory and internal-linking capabilities in your tool.
caveats: The subdirectory-vs-subdomain recommendation is the presenter's stated observation, not a published benchmark.
Tail questions may have very low volume; the value is being the only citation, not high traffic.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to AEO_ How to get ChatGPT to recommend your product _ Ethan Smith.docx

cards.title: Mine sales calls and support tickets for tail questions to answer
cards.summary: Tail questions are asked in chat and sales contexts but rarely covered; sourcing them from calls and support lets you become the sole citation.
cards.use_when: Building FAQ, help center or comparison content that answers low-volume but high-intent questions about your store's products or integrations.
steps: Collect questions that appear in sales calls and support interactions — these reveal the real use cases buyers ask about.

Identify questions where no competitor has published anything, such as the source's example of needing a meeting-transcription tool that integrates with Looker (solved via Otter plus Zapier plus BigQuery).
Write a plain, useful answer for each such question even if search volume looks near zero, because being the only source lets you win the citation.
Pair this with an open community Q&A where users can ask anything, so the tail keeps expanding without you having to guess all the questions in advance.
Cross-link these answers into your existing help center cluster so they are discoverable and connected.
caveats: Tail content is a long-tail bet; expect low individual traffic and value the citation position rather than volume.
The Looker example is illustrative of method, not a template solution for every integration question.

cards.title: Apply persuasion and behavioral-economics frameworks to growth tests
cards.summary: The source recommends drawing on psychology research — persuasion, emotional intelligence, dual-process thinking — as the basis for growth hypotheses instead of guessing.
cards.use_when: Designing A/B tests for product pages, offers, pricing, checkout or signup flows where you need a reason to believe a variant will outperform.
steps: Use frameworks from persuasion psychology (the source names Cialdini) to generate hypotheses about why a visitor would sign up or buy — scarcity, social proof, consistency, reciprocity, authority, liking.
Use emotional-intelligence research to understand how people feel when making a purchase decision, informing tone, reassurance and objection handling on product and checkout pages.
Apply dual-process thinking (fast vs. slow thinking) when designing pages: decide whether the buyer is in fast, intuitive mode or slow, deliberative mode and design accordingly.
Turn each framework into a testable hypothesis rather than treating it as a universal rule, and test it on your own store.
Read the source material behind these frameworks rather than only the popular summaries, since the source emphasizes that the frameworks are grounded in actual psychology research.
caveats: These are the source's reading recommendations and reasoning; no ecommerce conversion benchmarks are provided.
Persuasion tactics can backfire if applied manipulatively or without testing on your specific audience.

cards.title: Measure things that seem unmeasurable by finding proxies
cards.summary: The source recommends 'How to Measure Anything', which shows how to measure indirect concepts through observable proxies — like judging a conductor by standing ovations.
cards.use_when: Setting measurement for AEO, brand, content quality or other store outcomes where you lack a direct metric.
steps: Identify the concept you want to measure that lacks a clean metric (e.g., AEO impact, content usefulness, brand strength).
Find an observable proxy that correlates with it — the source's example: instead of surveying audiences, count standing ovations to judge an orchestra conductor.
Use the proxy consistently over time so you can detect direction of change, even if the absolute number is imperfect.
For an ecommerce AEO application, proxies could include citation appearances in LLM answers, click-throughs from answer modules, or branded search lift — measure whichever is observable to you.
Treat the proxy as a decision aid, not a precise measurement, and keep watching for a better proxy.
caveats: Proxies can be misleading if the correlation is weak; validate the proxy before relying on it for major decisions.
This is the source's reading recommendation, applied here by analogy to ecommerce AEO; the source did not give an ecommerce measurement example.

cards.title: Recognize LLM and search are converging into one experience
cards.summary: The source predicts search and LLMs will merge — Google adding AI overviews, LLMs adding maps and shopping carousels — into a single experience.
cards.use_when: Setting content and channel strategy for your store on a multi-year horizon rather than optimizing separately for classic search and LLMs.
steps: Observe the convergence in both directions: Google Search is adding LLM AI overviews, and LLMs are adding maps and shopping carousels.
Plan for a single optimized experience rather than two separate playbooks, since the surfaces are merging.

Identify the perverse incentives in this merged world (such as AI-generated content and scraping) and avoid building a strategy that depends on them, the way the source advises thinking about what a bad actor would do.
Invest in the things LLMs can be uniquely good at — memory of your past interactions, personalization, and eventually autonomous agents that make decisions without intervention.
For ecommerce, this points toward making product and feature data structured and answerable so it can be surfaced and acted on inside a converged assistant experience.
caveats: This is the source's forecast, not a measured fact; timing and exact form are uncertain.
Autonomous-agent commerce is presented as something that will eventually come, not something available for planning concrete campaigns today.

cards.title: Prepare product data for autonomous-agent purchasing
cards.summary: The source describes a future where LLMs, with full context on your preferences and reasoning, make purchase decisions without user intervention — like an executive assistant booking a trip.
cards.use_when: Structuring product attributes, pricing and integration data so an AI assistant can select and transact for a buyer without human steps.
steps: Understand the source's model: an assistant that deeply understands the buyer's preferences (ocean view, restaurant with music in the example), remembers everything, has context and reasoning, then makes decisions without intervention.
Anticipate that in this scenario the assistant, not the shopper, compares your product — so machine-readable attributes, availability, pricing and compatibility matter more than persuasion copy.
Make sure your product data clearly answers 'does this fit the use case' questions in structured, unambiguous form.
Ensure integration and compatibility facts (does it work with X) are documented, since assistant-driven decisions hinge on fit rather than brand persuasion.
Keep this as a forward-looking bet and continue optimizing current surfaces; the source presents autonomous agents as eventual, not immediate.
caveats: This is a forecast and speculative scenario, not an available channel; do not reallocate all effort to it now.
No ecommerce data point or benchmark is given for agent-driven purchasing.
